titre: The crater geology mistook for a volcano
accroche: For nearly seventy years, this Arizona hole was explained by a steam explosion. It was a meteorite impact.
contenu_vulgarise:
In Arizona, about thirty kilometers west of Winslow, a crater roughly 1.2 kilometers in diameter and nearly 170 meters deep has intrigued geologists since the late 19th century. Known today as Meteor Crater or Barringer Crater, it long carried an explanation very far from the one we know.

## A steam explosion

Grove Karl Gilbert, chief geologist of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), studies the site starting in the 1890s. He first considers a meteoritic origin, and even looks for a buried magnetic mass that would betray a block of iron left beneath the ground. Finding nothing convincing, he concludes a volcanic origin: an underground steam explosion, comparable to those observed in geothermal fields. Gilbert's authority weighs heavily, and this explanation prevails in the geological community for several decades.

## A mining engineer persists

Daniel Barringer, a mining engineer, discovers the site in 1902 and very quickly develops the opposite hypothesis: the crater is a meteorite impact, and a considerable mass of iron, potentially exploitable, should lie beneath its floor. In 1906, with Benjamin Tilghman, he publishes his arguments in the Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia. His company, the Standard Iron Company, drills the site from 1903 to 1929, swallowing more than $600,000, without ever reaching any metallic deposit. The astronomer Forest Ray Moulton will later calculate that most of the meteorite's mass vaporized on impact, which explains the failure, but does not yet convince the geological community of the crater's origin.

## The proof that comes from a mineral

The debate is not closed until 1960. The geologist Eugene Shoemaker, then a young researcher at the USGS, has sandstone samples collected at the crater analyzed by the mineralogist Edward Chao. Chao, with his colleague Beth Madsen, identifies coesite in them, a variety of quartz that forms only under extreme pressures. Far beyond what a steam explosion produces, such pressures are typical of a high-speed impact. The publication, on July 22, 1960, closes a debate nearly seventy years old.

## What the episode shifts

Neither Gilbert nor Barringer was wrong about everything: Gilbert had the right method, looking for a buried mass, without the right result; Barringer had the right origin without the right explanation for the absence of metal. It was a mineral, not shrewder geological reasoning, that finally settled it. The method developed on this occasion, spotting minerals that form only under extreme shock, has since been used to identify impact craters far less visible than the one in Arizona, including beneath layers of sediment or forest.

repere.texte: Grove Karl Gilbert (USGS) attributes the crater to a steam explosion in the 1890s. Daniel Barringer defends the meteoritic origin from 1906 and drills the site from 1903 to 1929 without finding any metal. The definitive proof, coesite, a mineral formed under extreme impact pressure, is not published until July 22, 1960, by Edward Chao, Eugene Shoemaker, and Beth Madsen.
repere.source: EARTH Magazine (American Geosciences Institute); Barringer Crater Company

carte.punch: This Arizona crater was mistaken for a volcano for nearly seventy years.
carte.idee: The USGS chief geologist explained it by a steam explosion. A mining engineer kept stubbornly looking for the meteorite beneath it, in vain: it had vaporized on impact. The proof did not come until 1960, from a mineral that forms only under extreme pressure.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Details on the Standard Iron Company's drilling and Forest Ray Moulton's calculation of the meteorite's vaporization.

quiz.question: How was the meteoritic origin of the Arizona crater definitively proven in 1960?
choix: By the identification of coesite, a mineral that forms only under extreme impact pressure
By the discovery of a metallic fragment buried beneath the crater floor
By radiometric dating of the rocks at the crater's rim
By direct comparison with the shape of other photographed lunar craters
quiz.explication: It was a mineral, coesite, identified by Edward Chao in samples collected by Eugene Shoemaker, that settled it: it forms only under extreme pressures, incompatible with a volcanic origin. No metallic fragment was ever found; the meteorite largely vaporized on impact.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Grove Karl Gilbert explain the crater's origin in the 1890s?
choix: By the fall of a comet that would have disintegrated entirely at the surface
By an underground steam explosion, comparable to those of geothermal fields
By the collapse of a karst cavity carved by groundwater
By an ancient landslide, later reshaped by wind erosion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gilbert had first considered a meteoritic origin and looked for a buried magnetic mass; having found nothing conclusive, he concluded an underground steam explosion.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Daniel Barringer's Standard Iron Company obtain after twenty-six years of drilling the site?
choix: A major iron deposit, later mined into the 1950s
Enough meteorite fragments to fund the drilling
Definitive geological proof of the crater's meteoritic origin
No metallic deposit, despite more than $600,000 spent
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Barringer's company drills the site from 1903 to 1929, swallowing more than $600,000, without ever reaching any exploitable metallic deposit.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the astronomer Forest Ray Moulton calculate to explain the failure of Barringer's drilling?
choix: That most of the meteorite's mass vaporized at the moment of impact
That the meteorite had deviated from its trajectory before hitting the ground
That the iron mass had dissolved in the local groundwater
That the crater resulted from two distinct impacts rather than a single body
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Moulton calculates that most of the meteorite's mass vaporized on impact, which explains the failure of the drilling without yet convincing the geological community.
